liturgical_day: Monday of the Twenty-third Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Stretch out your hand
theme: Christ reveals the Sabbath as a day for mercy, confronts hearts that turn law into accusation, and restores the hand that obeys his life-giving command.
introduction: The synagogue is full, but not everyone has come ready to receive the truth. Jesus teaches before a man whose right hand is withered, while the scribes and Pharisees watch for a violation they can use against him. Bede notices how their scrutiny twists every possible outcome: if Jesus does not heal, they can accuse him of cruelty or weakness; if he heals, they will accuse him of breaking the Sabbath. Christ refuses their trap by bringing the suffering man into the midst and asking what the holy day is for. Cyril of Alexandria returns to the Sabbath command itself. Rest was given as an act of mercy even toward servants and animals; it cannot truthfully be invoked against mercy for a human being. The question therefore exposes more than a faulty interpretation. It discloses whether the law is being received as God's gift or wielded as cover for envy. The man answers without argument. At Christ's command he stretches out the very hand that could not serve him, and obedience becomes the place of healing. Those who were watching for guilt see divine power and yet grow more hostile. The scene asks whether the presence of grace will open the heart or harden it further—and whether our own hands are ready to be stretched toward God and neighbor.
hero_alt: Jesus heals a man's withered right hand in the synagogue while scribes and Pharisees watch, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and restrained luminous geometry
closing_title: Let mercy reveal the law's purpose
closing: Jesus does not evade the hostile watchers, nor does he let their distorted use of the Sabbath determine the limits of compassion. He calls the man into the center, where hidden suffering and hidden malice alike are brought into the light. His question is deliberately sharp: refusing the good is not a neutral way of honoring God. When mercy is possible, the choice not to serve life already inclines toward destruction. The Fathers therefore read this healing at once as a defense of good works and as a sign of the soul's restoration. A hand is given for action—for generosity, protection, prayer, and service—but sin and self-concern can leave it spiritually contracted. Christ's command reaches precisely into that incapacity: stretch it out. The man does not wait to feel strength before obeying; in obedient extension, his hand is restored. Ambrose turns the miracle toward us by naming the movements of a healed hand: helping a neighbor, protecting the widow, defending the injured, giving to the poor, and asking pardon from God. These are not distractions from holy rest. They are signs that divine mercy has made us capable of good. Yet the final verse warns that a witnessed grace can still become an occasion for resistance. The Pharisees see life restored and answer with madness because envy has trained them to prefer accusation to wonder. Today, place before Christ whatever has become cramped, guarded, or fruitless. Hear his command not as humiliation but as creative mercy. Stretch out the hand he made, and let its restored work become praise.

verses.text: On another sabbath, he entered the synagogue and taught. There was a man whose right hand was withered.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose sees this healing as part of Christ's purpose to make the whole person sound. No human weakness lies outside the reach of the one who can restore every member.
verses.commentary: Ambrose introduces the scene by looking beyond an isolated cure. Christ intends to make the whole human person sound, and therefore he is able to restore each wounded member. The withered hand is not incidental to his mission but a concrete place where that saving purpose becomes visible. Jesus enters the synagogue and teaches before healing, joining truth and power in one work. The setting also makes the act public: amid the gathered people, bodily weakness will become a sign that the Lord's salvation reaches human life in its particular needs.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11

verses.text: The scribes and Pharisees watched to see whether he would heal on the sabbath, so that they might find an accusation against him.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede exposes the watchers' dishonest dilemma: they mean to accuse Jesus whether he heals or refrains. Their concern is not fidelity to the Sabbath but the manufacture of a charge.
verses.commentary: Bede says the scribes and Pharisees are no longer merely criticizing the disciples; they now watch the Master himself in order to construct a false accusation. Their design corrupts every possible outcome. If Jesus leaves the man unhealed, they can portray him as cruel or powerless. If he heals, they can charge him with violating the Sabbath. Such watching is the opposite of contemplation: it attends closely to Christ while refusing to seek truth. Bede's reading warns that religious language can conceal a verdict already chosen, making even mercy into evidence for condemnation.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11

verses.text: But he knew their thoughts and said to the man who had the withered hand, “Rise and stand in the midst.” And he rose and stood there.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril says Christ brings the man forward while fully knowing the hidden thoughts around him. The visible suffering might yet awaken pity and cool the Pharisees' cruel passion.
verses.commentary: Cyril emphasizes that Jesus searches hearts and already knows the accusation forming within his opponents. Nevertheless, he calls the man to rise and stand in the midst. The command makes the need impossible to keep at a safe distance: the watchers must face a suffering neighbor, not merely debate a rule in abstraction. Cyril suggests that Christ presents the man openly in the hope that visible affliction may stir pity and calm their cruel passion. The man's immediate obedience also prepares the miracle; he accepts exposure and stands where the Lord has summoned him.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11

verses.text: Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you: Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?”
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril returns the dispute to the Sabbath's merciful purpose. A command that grants rest to servants and animals cannot be interpreted as forbidding mercy to a suffering person.
verses.commentary: Cyril calls Christ's question especially useful because it forces the accusation into the light. If doing good on the Sabbath is lawful, then the healing cannot be condemned. If good is forbidden and a person's welfare must be neglected, the critic has turned the law itself into something merciless. Cyril recalls that Sabbath rest was commanded for servants and even cattle. The institution therefore bears God's compassion within it. One who allows rest for an animal cannot reasonably deny mercy to a human being afflicted by severe disease. Jesus fulfills the holy day's purpose by saving life.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11

verses.text: Looking around at them all, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose makes the restored hand a summons to active mercy. A hand becomes whole as it reaches toward God and outward to protect, assist, and give.
verses.commentary: Ambrose hears Christ's command as more than the end of one man's disability. The restored hand reveals what a healthy human power is for. Stretch it out, he says, to help a neighbor, protect the widow, defend someone suffering injustice, and give to the poor who asks. Stretch it also toward the Lord in prayer for the pardon of sins. Avarice and sacrilege can contract a hand that appears physically sound, because they prevent it from doing the good for which it was made. In extending the hand through obedient charity, it is healed.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11

verses.text: They were filled with madness and spoke with one another about what they might do to Jesus.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril contrasts the divine work of healing with envy that answers life by plotting death. The miracle is clear; it is the watchers' desire that has become disordered.
verses.commentary: Cyril confronts the terrible reversal in the final verse. The Pharisee sees a divine worker freeing the sick by heavenly power, yet envy causes him to breathe out death. The healed hand should have prompted wonder, gratitude, and recognition of God's mercy. Instead, Christ's opponents turn from the restored man toward plans against the healer. Their madness does not arise from lack of evidence but from resistance to the good placed before them. Cyril's contrast exposes envy as spiritually destructive: it can witness another's deliverance and experience that gift as a threat rather than a reason for praise.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:6–11
